As of 1242 AM EST Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Modest pressure gradients this evening have kept south 
winds going overnight, resulting in much warmer conditions compared 
to the last few nights over the forecast area. Despite starting out 
much warmer, increasing cloud cover will keep temperatures in the 
mid 50s to lower 60s, except mid 60s across the St. Lawrence Valley. 
Coastal area of low pressure will pass far enough east to graze 
eastern Vermont. A few high res members suggest a little activity 
developing on the cirrus periphery in the northern Champlain Valley, 
but by and large, we will miss out on wetting rains. Forecast trends 
reach a quarter inch mainly for the far southeastern tip of Windsor 
County, and quickly taper to a few hundredths or no accumulations 
west of the Greens. A sharp cold front will shift east soon after 
the coastal low passes east on Monday. It could generate a few 
showers, mainly along the international border and mix with snow 
late in the evening above 3000 feet.

Brisk northwest winds will follow the front as a strong high builds 
in to replace the falling pressures of Monday. Widespread 20-30 mph, 
locally to 35 mph along the northeastern tip of the Adirondacks 
(like Ellenburg), will prevail into the overnight hours. These winds 
will quickly bring in some cooler temperatures into the 20s to near 
30 across the region. Seasonably cool temperatures around 5-10 
degrees below normal will hang around through Wednesday, and winds 
will subside during the day on Tuesday as a large near 1040mb 
surface high sets up overhead.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The forecast for Thanksgiving day and towards the 
weekend remains unchanged as a widespread precipitation event 
remains increasingly likely. Synoptically, a closed upper level low 
will dip south from the Dakotas into the Ohio Valley early to mid 
week, phasing with a southern stream low from the Deep South. This 
upper low will occlude somewhere over the Great Lakes, while a 
coastal low is expected to develop off the Florida coast mid week as 
well. Models continue to struggle with how these systems interact by 
Thanksgiving, but a subtle trend so far has been towards a stronger 
coastal low tracking up the east coast, while the upper level low 
spins over the eastern Great Lakes. Moreover, given the positioning 
of the upper low to the coastal low, colder air will be at a premium 
as Arctic air will remain largely locked north of the border. For 
us, this means a trend towards a warmer system, with more widespread 
cold rain favored. Supporting this will be good warm moist air 
advection off the Atlantic by the coastal low. That said, as our 
strong high lifts to the northeast on Thanksgiving day, some cold 
air may linger at the onset in our climatologically favored 
locations in the NEK and northern St. Lawrence Valley (i.e. Newport, 
VT and Massena, NY) before scouring out overnight Thursday. 
Probabilities for wintry precipitation have decreased for much of 
the area in general with probabilities for 850mb temperatures less 
than 0C in both the Euro and GFS ensembles only 20-30% at the onset 
of precipitation during the day on Thanksgiving. A brief period of 
wintry mix may be still be possible in the NEK and northern St. 
Lawrence Valley, though, late Thanksgiving day, though impacts will 
be minimal due to the short duration of any wintry mix before 
transitioning to all rain overnight. All that is only applicable, 
however, if we even see precipitation, as there are still a number 
of ensemble members that give us a dry slot between the coastal 
system and the upper low. Given recent model predictability with the 
current coastal system, this dry slot is still a real possibility. 
Regardless, the system will be associated with a strong jet (60+kt 
around 850mb), so expect some gusty winds along the terrain, with 
uncertainty remaining in how much these gusts mix to the valleys due 
to precipitation contamination. We'll continue to watch trends 
closely as the Thanksgiving holiday approaches, and we urge you to 
do the same, especially if you have outdoor or travel plans.
